questions.q: Give a reason for the following: $p$-nitrophenol is more acidic than $p$-methylphenol.
questions.solution:
The acidity of a phenol is decided by how **stable** its conjugate base, the phenoxide ion, is. Anything that spreads the negative charge away from the oxygen makes the phenoxide more stable and the phenol more acidic.

**$p$-nitrophenol.** The nitro group is strongly **electron-withdrawing**, both by the inductive effect ($-I$) and, more importantly, by resonance ($-R$). Being in the **para** position, it is perfectly placed to accept the negative charge through the ring: the charge can be delocalised right onto the oxygen atoms of the $-\text{NO}_2$ group.

The $p$-nitrophenoxide ion is therefore **strongly stabilised**, and $p$-nitrophenol readily gives up its proton.

**$p$-methylphenol.** The methyl group is **electron-releasing** ($+I$ and hyperconjugation). It pushes electron density **into** the ring, intensifying the negative charge on the phenoxide oxygen rather than relieving it.

That **destabilises** the conjugate base, so $p$-methylphenol holds on to its proton more tightly.

**Conclusion.** An electron-withdrawing substituent stabilises the phenoxide and raises acidity; an electron-releasing one does the opposite. Hence $p$-nitrophenol ($\text{p}K_a \approx 7 \cdot 1$) is far more acidic than $p$-methylphenol ($\text{p}K_a \approx 10 \cdot 2$), with phenol itself ($\approx 10 \cdot 0$) in between.

questions.q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol because:
questions.solution:
On losing a proton, phenol gives the **phenoxide ion**, whose negative charge is delocalised over the ring by resonance.

Ethoxide has no such escape route — the charge sits entirely on one oxygen, and the electron-releasing ethyl group makes matters worse.

A stabilised conjugate base means a stronger acid: $\text{p}K_{a}$ about $10$ for phenol against $16$ for ethanol.
options: the phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance
it has a higher boiling point

questions.q: The Lucas reagent distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols by the:
questions.solution:
Lucas reagent is concentrated HCl with anhydrous $\text{ZnCl}_{2}$. The alkyl chloride formed is insoluble, so the solution goes **turbid**.

**Tertiary:** immediately. **Secondary:** in about 5 minutes. **Primary:** only on heating.

The order follows carbocation stability, since the reaction goes by $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$.
options: time taken for turbidity to appear

questions.q: Williamson's synthesis of ethers works best with:
questions.solution:
The alkoxide is both a good nucleophile and a strong base. With a **primary** halide it substitutes cleanly ($\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$).

With a tertiary halide it acts as a base instead and **eliminates**, giving an alkene rather than the ether.

So to make **tert**-butyl methyl ether, use **tert**-butoxide with methyl iodide — put the bulk on the alkoxide, never on the halide.

questions.q: Phenol treated with $\text{CO}_{2}$ and $\text{NaOH}$ under pressure, then acid, gives:
questions.solution:
This is the **Kolbe–Schmitt reaction**, giving **salicylic acid** (2-hydroxybenzoic acid).

The phenoxide ion is electron-rich enough to attack carbon dioxide, and the ortho position is favoured because the sodium ion holds the $\text{CO}_{2}$ close to the oxygen.

Acetylating the product gives aspirin.

questions.q: A secondary alcohol on oxidation gives:
questions.solution:
A secondary alcohol has one hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, so it stops at the **ketone** — there is no further hydrogen to remove.

A primary alcohol gives an aldehyde and then, with a strong oxidant, a carboxylic acid. A tertiary alcohol has no such hydrogen at all and resists oxidation, unless the conditions are harsh enough to break the carbon skeleton.

questions.q: How many structural isomeric alcohols are possible for $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{OH}$?
questions.solution:
Butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol — $\mathbf{4}$.

Two primary, one secondary and one tertiary, which makes this set the standard demonstration of the Lucas test.

questions.q: Find the molar mass of phenol, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$, in g/mol. (C $= 12$, H $= 1$, O $= 16$.)
How many isomeric ethers are possible with the formula $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$?
questions.solution:
Methoxypropane, 2-methoxypropane (methyl isopropyl ether) and ethoxyethane — $\mathbf{3}$.

$\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ also has four alcohol isomers, making seven in all — ethers and alcohols are **functional isomers** of one another.

questions.q: Find the degree of unsaturation for phenol, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{6}\text{O}$.
questions.solution:
Degree of unsaturation $= \dfrac{2(6) + 2 - 6}{2} = \dfrac{8}{2} = \mathbf{4}$.

Three from the ring's double bonds and one from the ring itself — exactly what a benzene ring always contributes.

questions.q: How many bromine atoms are introduced when phenol reacts with excess bromine water?
questions.solution:
Phenol gives an immediate white precipitate of **2,4,6-tribromophenol**, so $\mathbf{3}$.

No catalyst is needed — the $-\text{OH}$ group activates the ring so strongly that all three available positions substitute at once. Benzene itself would need a Lewis acid and would stop at one.

questions.q: Explain why phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol but weaker than carboxylic acids, and how substituents on the ring change its acidity.
questions.solution:
**Phenol vs ethanol.** The phenoxide ion delocalises its negative charge over the ortho and para positions of the ring, which stabilises it. Ethoxide cannot do this, and the electron-releasing ethyl group intensifies the charge.

$\text{p}K_{a}$: phenol $10$, ethanol $16$.

**Phenol vs carboxylic acids.** In a carboxylate ion the charge is shared between **two equivalent oxygen atoms** — both resonance structures are identical and equally good. In phenoxide the charge is pushed onto **carbon** atoms, which are far less able to hold it, and those structures also destroy the ring's aromaticity.

$\text{p}K_{a}$ of acetic acid is about $4.7$ — roughly a hundred thousand times more acidic than phenol.

**Substituent effects.**

• **Electron-withdrawing groups** ($-\text{NO}_{2}$, $-\text{CN}$, halogens) spread the charge further and **increase** acidity. Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) is as strong as a mineral acid.

• **Electron-releasing groups** ($-\text{CH}_{3}$, $-\text{OCH}_{3}$) push charge onto the oxygen and **decrease** acidity. Cresol is weaker than phenol.

The effect is strongest from the **ortho and para** positions, where resonance can reach; a meta substituent works only by induction and matters far less.

questions.q: Describe the dehydration of alcohols to alkenes, with the mechanism and the order of reactivity.
questions.solution:
**Reaction.** With concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ at $443$ K, ethanol gives ethene:

$\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4},\;443\text{ K}} \text{CH}_{2}{=}\text{CH}_{2} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$

**Mechanism (E1, three steps).**

**Step 1 — protonation.** The acid protonates the $-\text{OH}$, turning a terrible leaving group ($\text{OH}^{-}$) into an excellent one ($\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$). This is the whole purpose of the acid.

**Step 2 — loss of water** gives a carbocation. Slow, and rate-determining.

**Step 3 — loss of a proton** from the adjacent carbon forms the double bond.

**Order of reactivity:** tertiary $>$ secondary $>$ primary, following carbocation stability. Tertiary alcohols dehydrate at $360$ K with dilute acid; primary ones need $443$ K and concentrated acid.

**Orientation:** Saytzeff's rule — the more substituted alkene dominates.

**A warning:** carbocations rearrange. 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol dehydrates to 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, because a methyl group shifts to give a more stable cation before the proton is lost.

questions.q: How would you distinguish between (a) phenol and ethanol, (b) primary and tertiary alcohols?
questions.solution:
**(a) Phenol from ethanol.**

1. **Neutral $\text{FeCl}_{3}$:** phenol gives a **violet** colour (an iron–phenoxide complex); ethanol gives nothing.

2. **Bromine water:** phenol gives an immediate **white precipitate** of 2,4,6-tribromophenol; ethanol does not react.

3. **$\text{NaOH}$ solution:** phenol dissolves as sodium phenoxide (it is acidic enough); ethanol does not.

4. **Litmus:** phenol is weakly acidic; ethanol is neutral.

**(b) Primary from tertiary alcohol.**

1. **Lucas test:** the tertiary alcohol turns the solution turbid **at once**; the primary one only on heating.

2. **Victor Meyer test:** primary gives a **blood-red** colour, secondary blue, tertiary **colourless**.

3. **Oxidation with acidified $\text{K}_{2}\text{Cr}_{2}\text{O}_{7}$:** the primary alcohol turns the orange solution green (giving an aldehyde, then an acid); the tertiary alcohol leaves it orange.

For a written answer, give the reagent, what you see, and what it means — all three.

questions.q: Describe the reaction of ethers with HI, and explain why the products differ between an alkyl ether and an aryl alkyl ether.
questions.solution:
**With an alkyl ether.** Ethers are cleaved by hot concentrated HI:

$\text{R–O–R}' + \text{HI} \to \text{R–I} + \text{R}'\text{–OH}$

The iodide attacks the **smaller, less hindered** alkyl group ($\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$), so methyl ethyl ether gives methyl iodide and ethanol.

With a **tertiary** group the mechanism switches to $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ and the tertiary halide forms instead, since its carbocation is so stable.

**With an aryl alkyl ether — anisole.**

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{–O–CH}_{3} + \text{HI} \to \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} + \text{CH}_{3}\text{I}$

The products are **always phenol and the alkyl iodide**, never iodobenzene and methanol.

**Why.** The bond between oxygen and the aromatic carbon has partial double-bond character from resonance and is far too strong to break; and the $sp^{2}$ carbon cannot undergo $\text{S}_{\text{N}}2$ attack at all. The iodide has only one bond it can reach, so it takes the methyl group every time.
